status_summary: Executive Order 14159 (signed 2025-01-20, 90 FR 8443) directed State and DHS to use INA 243(d) sanctions to the fullest extent of the law; no formally cited 243(d) action was found in the Federal Register. The visible measures are entry proclamations under INA 212(f) and 215(a): Proclamation 10949 (signed 2025-06-04, effective 2025-06-09) and Proclamation 10998 (signed 2025-12-16, effective 2026-01-01) fully suspend entry for 19 countries and partially suspend immigrant and B, F, M and J visas for 20 more, citing in part overstay rates and, for five countries, refusal to take back removable nationals; this design differs from country-specific 243(d) sanctions and goes beyond them in scope. State's visa bond final rule (91 FR 48757) made the B-1/B-2 bond program permanent on 2026-08-03, and a final rule published 2026-03-11 (91 FR 11891, effective 2026-04-10) requires Diversity Visa entrants to give valid passport information. On 2026-08-21 the Southern District of New York vacated the 75-country immigrant visa pause, and on 2026-08-28 the Northern District of California temporarily vacated, pending further litigation, the diversity visa pause, the 75-country pause and a USCIS hold; neither order addresses Proclamation 10998 or INA 243(d).

timeline.event: Executive Order 14159, section 13, directed the Secretaries of State and Homeland Security to implement the sanctions authorized by INA 243(d) to the fullest extent allowed, to build acceptance of removable nationals into diplomatic negotiations, and to weigh a country's delays in verifying identities (signed 2025-01-20; published 2025-01-29 at 90 FR 8443).

Proclamation 10949 suspended entry for nationals of 12 countries and partially for 7 (immigrant visas plus B, F, M and J), effective 2025-06-09, citing among other things overstay rates and refusal to accept removable nationals (90 FR 24497, published 2025-06-10).
State published a temporary rule creating a visa bond pilot program for B-1/B-2 applicants from designated countries; the pilot ran from 2025-08-20 to 2026-08-05.

Proclamation 10998 (90 FR 59717, published 2025-12-19) continues the full suspension for 12 countries (section 2) and the partial suspension for 4 (section 3), adds full suspension for 7 countries (section 4: Burkina Faso, Laos, Mali, Niger, Sierra Leone, South Sudan, Syria) plus Palestinian Authority travel documents, and adds partial suspension for 16 (section 5), for 19 full and 20 partial countries by the record's count; effective 2026-01-01; the Secretary of State reports every 180 days (section 7). Sections 4 and 5 cite refusal to accept removable nationals for five countries.

State publishes a final rule (91 FR 11891, effective 2026-04-10, starting with DV-2027) requiring Diversity Visa entrants to provide valid passport information and a scan of the passport page, to confirm identities earlier, support vetting and curb fraudulent third-party entries.

State's final rule (91 FR 48757, effective 2026-08-03) made the visa bond program permanent for B-1/B-2 applicants from State-designated countries, with bonds of up to 20,000 dollars set by the consular officer, finalizing the pilot program that began on 2025-08-20.

The Southern District of New York (Judge Jeannette Vargas, Catholic Legal Immigration Network v. Rubio, No. 26-cv-00858-JAV) grants plaintiffs partial summary judgment and vacates State's pause on immigrant visa issuance for nationals of 75 countries (announced 2026-01-14, effective 2026-01-21, implemented by a cable directing refusals under INA 221(g) on public-charge grounds). The court holds the policy contrary to law and beyond the Secretary's authority, including under the INA's nationality nondiscrimination provision, rejects a remand-only remedy, and does not address Proclamation 10998 or INA 243(d); news summaries say Proclamation 10998 was not affected.
timeline.source: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York

timeline.event: The Northern District of California (Judge Edward J. Davila, Medani v. Trump, No. 5:26-cv-06332-EJD) grants in part class certification and a preliminary injunction motion, temporarily vacates, pending further litigation, the State diversity visa pause, the State 75-country immigrant visa pause and the USCIS diversity visa hold (pp. 21-23), orders State and USCIS to reconsider or resume adjudication to the extent practicable for the rest of FY2026, certifies three subclasses, finds the policies likely arbitrary and capricious under the APA, and requires a joint status report by 2026-09-18; the order has no stay or appeal language.

A State Department visa news notice (last updated 2026-08-31) says that, as of 2026-08-28 and under the court's order in Medani v. Trump, the December 2025 pause on diversity visa issuance is no longer in effect; the same page also carries text announcing a pause on all diversity visa issuance with no separate start date, tied to a review of screening and vetting.

title: Enforce visa reciprocity and INA 243(d) sanctions and review sensitive visa programs
uncertainties: No actual State or DHS invocation of INA 243(d) was verified; the Federal Register record of EO 14159 section 13 is the only primary document on 243(d), and the February 2026 use against Cuban officials comes from a secondary immigration-news site that cites no government source. 9 FAM 601.12 (fam.state.gov, changed 2023-12-08), read on 2026-10-26, provides that 243(d) discontinuations are made by Secretary's order and communicated by cable, so (inference) a sanction would not necessarily appear in the Federal Register; it names no sanctioned country. Reciprocity-schedule changes and student-visa vetting changes were not researched, nor were court challenges to the proclamations. The 19 and 20 country counts are this tracker's tally from the proclamation text (Turkmenistan counted among the partial group; Laos and Sierra Leone moved from partial to full). The 75-country pause dates (announced 2026-01-14, effective 2026-01-21) come from the S.D.N.Y. opinion (mirror on media.nilc.org); State's 2026-08-28 filing in that case was not located, and the report that the pause ended rests on a law-firm blog. The State diversity visa notice, read through an automated summary, both says the December 2025 pause ended on 2026-08-28 and retains text announcing a pause on all diversity visa issuances (interviews continue, no visas issued) tied to a screening review; whether that text is the original December 2025 notice left on the page or a new pause was not resolved. The Medani order is a temporary vacatur with a joint status report due 2026-09-18; later proceedings were not checked. The Medani order was read only in a copy on courthousenews.com; searches on 2026-10-26 found no copy on CourtListener or the court's site, and a Clearinghouse case page that appeared in results was not opened. The December 2025 pause start date (a law firm gives 2025-12-23) was not confirmed on a State page. The Federal Register API (EO 14159, Proclamations 10949 and 10998, the diversity visa final rule 91 FR 11891 and the visa bond final rule 91 FR 48757) confirmed numbers, signing and publication dates; a Federal Register search for notices citing section 243(d) returned only EO 14159 and an unrelated DHS proposed rule. The Medani order PDF was read and gives two start dates for the December 2025 diversity visa pause (2025-12-20 and 2025-12-23) and two for the 75-country pause. Two reports are not government actions and appear only as sources: VisaVerge (February 2026, a claimed 243(d) use against Cuban officials with no government citation) and the Manifest Law blog (2026-08-28 to 2026-08-31, on State's compliance and a worldwide immigrant visa appointment pause).
